subject: mathematics
question_text: Show that cos²(π/10) + cos²(4π/10) + cos²(6π/10) + cos²(9π/10) = 2.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.109 — from the book's separate "STAR QUESTIONS PLUS" bank, answer 173. That bank (book pp.98-111, answers 142-180) sits AFTER all the numbered chapters and is organised by chapter rather than forming part of any chapter's own inventory; it is authored into this unit because that is where the question belongs on the paper (founder decision 2026-08-22). SECTION: classed SAQ on its length and shape. The bank prints no mark cut, so this classification is OURS. Printed appearances: AP 22. None of these four angles is standard, and none needs to be. The two larger ones turn into sines of the two smaller ones, and then Pythagoras closes it. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — the bank prints no [N Marks] tags anywhere. The shapes used follow the splits the book DOES print elsewhere: 1+1 for a 2-mark VSAQ (answers 100, 101 on book p.82), 1+1+1+1 or 1+2+1 for a 4-mark SAQ (answers 58, 59 on p.63 and 61 on p.64), and the granular split for a 7-mark LAQ (answer 32 on p.44). This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — name each move in order.

steps.label: Convert to degrees
steps.margin_note: First mark. π radians is 180°, so π/10 is 18°. The four angles are 18°, 72°, 108° and 162°.

recall.must_convey: That the four angles are 18°, 72°, 108° and 162°.
accept: pi by ten is eighteen degrees so the angles are eighteen seventy two one hundred and eight and one sixty two
convert the radians to degrees first
the four angles in degrees are eighteen seventy two one oh eight and one sixty two
pi by ten ante eighteen degrees
change to degrees

steps.why: Degrees make the 90° shift in the next step easy to see. The proof works in radians too, but the pattern is harder to spot there.
common_mistakes: Working in radians and missing the π/2 shifts.

steps.label: Rewrite the two larger angles
steps.margin_note: Second mark. 108° = 90° + 18° and 162° = 90° + 72° — each larger angle is 90° more than one of the smaller two.

accept: one oh eight is ninety plus eighteen and one sixty two is ninety plus seventy two
each larger angle is ninety more than one of the smaller ones
rewrite the two large angles with a ninety degree shift
ninety plus eighteen, ninety plus seventy two
shift the two larger angles by ninety

steps.why: The four angles were chosen so that they pair up under a 90° shift. Spotting that pairing is the whole question.
common_mistakes: Writing 108° as 180° − 72°, which works but leads to a longer route.

steps.label: Use cos(90° + θ) = −sin θ
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The shift turns each cosine into a negative sine — and the SQUARE removes the minus sign entirely.
lines: cos(90° + θ) = −sin θ, and squaring removes the sign:

recall.must_convey: That cos(90° + θ) = −sin θ, and squaring makes the two terms sin²18° and sin²72°.
accept: cos of ninety plus theta is minus sine theta and squaring removes the minus so they become sin squared
the two large terms become sin squared eighteen and sin squared seventy two
the square kills the negative sign
square kabatti minus poddi, sin square avthundi
convert the cosines to sines

steps.why: The minus would matter if the terms were not squared. Because they are, only the size carries through — which is what makes the pairing work.
common_mistakes: Keeping the minus sign after squaring.

steps.label: Pair by Pythagoras
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Regroup so each pair shares an angle: cos²18° + sin²18° = 1 and cos²72° + sin²72° = 1.

recall.must_convey: That regrouping gives two Pythagorean pairs, each equal to 1, so the sum is 2.
accept: group each cosine with the sine of the same angle so each pair is one and the total is two
cos squared plus sin squared is one for each angle
one plus one is two
prathi angle ki cos square plus sin square one, so total two
the answer is two

steps.why: The regrouping is the point — the terms are not in Pythagorean pairs as first written, and rearranging them is what makes the identity apply.
common_mistakes: Trying to find the numerical value of cos 18°.
